title: When to see the Orionid meteor shower in the Mid-South this week
excerpt: This week, you'll want to look up to the stars for the peak of the Orionid meteor shower.
content:
This week, you'll want to look up to the stars for the peak of the Orionid meteor shower.

The cause? A comet that will actually be billions of miles away.

That's right — the Orionids are actually caused by dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet. As Earth moves through the debris field, the result is a spectacular display of "Shooting stars" soaring across the night sky.

With dry conditions expected here in the Mid-South, and very little, if any, cloud cover, we will have ideal viewing conditions. In fact, we could see up to ten to twenty meteors, or "shooting stars", per hour streaking across the night sky, at speeds over forty miles per second.

So, where will you want to look to see this?

Well, the meteors can actually appear anywhere in the sky, but the reason why this is called the Orionid meteor shower is because the meteors appear to radiate from the Orion constellation, which is in the southeastern sky. One viewing tip — don't look directly at the constellation. Look forty to ninety degrees away from Orion for longer, more dramatic streaks.

Now, let's answer the "when" you should be looking for this.

The Orionids peak Wednesday night into Thursday morning. However, we will have a bright waxing gibbous moon Wednesday night, so viewing may be obscured due to a bit of light pollution.

Severe Weather Center 13 narrowed down the best time for viewing to be between moonset at around 3:30 a.m., and dawn at about 7 a.m. Thursday morning. So, if you are an early morning riser, take a glance out your window on Thursday — you may be in for a celestial treat.
